summary: For ages 7–9, teach the eye as an ordered light-processing chain that ends in the brain, plus one live observable response: the pupil reflex. Children trace light pupil→lens→retina→optic nerve→brain (each part named by its one job), observe the pupil changing size with brightness, and learn that the eye DETECTS light while the brain INTERPRETS it into what we 'see'. Core conceptual targets: seeing is a sequence ending in the brain (not the eye alone), the pupil is a hole whose size changes (not a coloured part), and light travels INTO the eye (not out of it). Keep to named parts; leave lens focal-length/inversion physics for later.
misconceptions: 'The eye sees / makes the picture' — missing that the eye detects light and the BRAIN interprets it.
'Light comes OUT of the eyes to see things' — the ancient 'extramission' idea; light goes INTO the eye.
'The pupil is a black dot/part' — rather than an opening that lets light in and changes size.
'The pupil changes colour' — confusing the pupil (the hole) with the iris (the coloured ring).
'The lens is like glasses that magnify' — rather than focusing light onto the retina.
'You see the whole scene instantly and perfectly' — missing that the retina detects and the brain assembles the image (sets up illusions later).

activities.title: Drive the light's journey through the eye
steps: Starting from a light source, trace the path in order and name each part by its one job: pupil (lets light in), lens (focuses light), retina (detects light), optic nerve (carries signals), brain (interprets the picture).
Using a model or diagram where brightness can be changed (e.g. a slider), make the light dim and bright and watch the pupil widen and narrow in response.

Follow light rays streaming through the pupil, the lens bending them to a sharp focus on the retina, and a signal firing up the optic nerve to a brain icon that 'lights up' with the interpreted image.
Tap or point to each part to pause and state its single job; push the light to 'too dim' and 'too bright' extremes and say why the pupil adjusts.
Say in your own words what the eye does versus what the brain does.
activities.insight: Seeing is a causal chain, not scattered labels: light enters, is focused, is detected by the retina, and only becomes the picture you 'see' when the brain interprets the signal. The pupil is a hole that changes size to control how much light enters.

activities.title: Watch the pupil reflex live (predict–observe–explain)
steps: In pairs in a normally lit room, predict whether your partner's pupils will get BIGGER or smaller when a moderate light (an ordinary torch or room light turned toward them — never shone directly into the eyes at close range) is used, and say WHY before looking.

As a gentler alternative that needs no extra light, have your partner cup their hands over their eyes for about 20 seconds, then uncover, and predict what their pupils will look like the instant they uncover.
Observe what actually happens, then compare it with your prediction.
Explain the result: what is the pupil doing, and why?
activities.insight: The pupil shrinks in bright light (to let less in) and widens in dim light or right after darkness (to gather more). The pupil is a light-control opening whose size is automatically adjusted.

activities.title: Which way does light travel? The dark-room argument
steps: Consider: in a completely dark room with no light at all, you can't see a thing even with your eyes wide open. Explain why not.
Commit to a direction: does light travel OUT of your eyes onto things, or FROM things INTO your eyes? Say which, and give your reason.
Explain the full account of how you end up seeing an object, from the object to the picture in your mind.
Discuss a tricky case: a cat's eyes seem to 'glow' in the dark — does that mean the cat's eyes make their own light to see with?
activities.insight: Seeing needs light to travel from objects INTO the eye; the eye is a receiver, not an emitter. With no light entering, the retina has nothing to detect — which is why a dark room is unseeable.

activities.title: Pupil, not iris: name the opening
steps: Look at your own eyes in a mirror, or at a partner's eyes, and point to the pupil (the black opening) and the iris (the coloured ring).
State which part is the HOLE that lets light in and which is the coloured ring that changes the hole's size.
Explain what changes when the pupil 'gets bigger' — is it a colour change or a size change of the opening?
activities.insight: The pupil is an opening (a hole) that lets light in and changes size; the iris is the coloured ring that adjusts it. The pupil does not change colour.

activities.title: Consolidate: sequence, match, and predict
steps: Put the light path in the correct order: pupil → lens → retina → optic nerve → brain.
Match each part to its one job (pupil—lets light in; lens—focuses light; retina—detects light; optic nerve—carries signals; brain—interprets the image).
Given a light level (bright or dim), predict whether the pupil will be smaller or bigger and explain why.
activities.insight: A learner can reliably name the parts, order the sequence, and predict the pupil's response by light level.

checkQuestion: In a completely dark room with no light at all, you can't see a thing, even with your eyes wide open. Why not? For seeing to happen, which way does the light have to travel — out of your eyes onto things, or from things into your eyes? Explain how you end up seeing an object.
checkAnswer: You can't see in the dark because seeing needs light to travel FROM objects INTO your eyes — your eyes don't send anything out. Light bounces off the object, enters through the pupil, the lens focuses it onto the retina at the back, and the retina sends signals along the optic nerve to the brain, which interprets the image. With no light entering, the retina has nothing to detect.
